utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, everybody. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So today we are going to hear the next witness. Are there any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. I hope you could remember is that our concern with this witness because from your 65 ter filings we found that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- he will testify to the things he saw are most the same with the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's the operative word "almost." It's the part that's not quite the same that I'm trying to get out, Your Honour, but there's going to be some interesting things, and I'm mindful of the Court's admonitions and concerns truly, and I'm going to streamline this entire case as much as I can, but I do intend to try a case that is going to be helpful for your decision-making at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could please tell us what your name is.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Srbislav Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if you could tell us your name letter by letter. Your last name.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: D-a-v-i-d-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, do you have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do. It's Buco, B-u-c-o.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, everything we're saying has to be translated so one, you need to speak slowly, and two, if you could speak loud enough so they can hear you in the booth, okay?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Davidovic, if you could please tell us, where are you from?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how long have you lived in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the day I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That would make it how many years?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fifty-seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I take it you were also educated there.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was. I completed the primary and the secondary school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: After secondary school did you get any further education?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did. I graduated from the secondary -- from the high teaching school, teacher's school in Bijeljina. After the teacher's school I graduated from the paedagogical academy in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how many years altogether was that?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Primary school, eight years; secondary school, four years; higher school, two years. That makes it 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Davidovic, after you completed your education, what was your first job?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I worked as a teacher, a teacher of the first four years in the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to speak slowly and clearly so they can hear you, because everything needs to be translated, sir. And just try to relax. I know you're nervous. Now, how long did you teach?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I taught from 1968 until 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And after that what job did you hold?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that I was appointed by the municipal assembly to the post of deputy head for internal affairs in the secretariat of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is that with the police force?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you were working for the Bratunac police in that capacity. How long did you work for the Bratunac police?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: One term of office. That's four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us just very briefly what your functions were when you held that job.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: My duties as deputy head of the secretariat for internal affairs in Bratunac involved being the chief of section for general administrative and legal affairs. That is one department. And my second department was in charge of the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Just very briefly, when we're talking about reserve police force, what are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The general secretariat for internal affairs of Bratunac included also the reserve police force. The strength of reserve police force in our secretariat was 300. Conceptually speaking, that falls under the concept of general People's Defence -- All People's Defence. By the law of 1978, reserve police forces were established. Their role was to act in emergency situations and in cases of immediate danger of war wherein they would be activated and discharge police duties. In the municipality of Bratunac, there were 13 local communes and the same number of reserve police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was this an obligatory duty for those individuals that were chosen to become part of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was obligatory. It was their wartime assignment, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was it -- I'm sorry. Go ahead. You wanted to supplement your --

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The secretariat for national defence would assign persons who have completed their military service to the reserve police force, and that was their wartime assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how long were you -- after you -- you told us you were with the Bratunac police for four years. After that job, where did you move on to?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: After my term of office was over, I was appointed director of the national university, or the people's university, rather, in Bratunac. That is a cultural institution which within it's purview had the national -- sorry, town library, the cinema, and implemented part of the educational programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how long did you hold that job?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was on that post from 1974 until the war began in 1992. That is where the war found me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you at some point in time become involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were you a member of a party?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Socialist Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Is that the same as the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. The abbreviation is SDP. The acronym is SDP. I was not a member of the SDS then. I was a member of the SDP. It's the former League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was my next question. We're talking about you being a member of the Communist Party. As a member, did you hold any positions at any point in time in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1978, at the session of the municipal assembly of Bratunac, I was elected vice-president of the municipal assembly, and I stayed in that post for two years, until 1980, when I was appointed to my police functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we move on, did the SDS and the SDP get along as parties?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose they did not have the same platform, and they were in fact fierce political enemies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you hold any other posts other than the one that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the SDP, I was a member of the Municipal Committee, and that was in the period from 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1988, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about IN 1995? Did you hold any posts at that particular period?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the municipality. You mean politically speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Politically speaking. That's what we're talking about. What was your -- what was your position?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was president of the Executive Board of the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How long had you been -- how long had you been in that position?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that position, I was from the 15th of October, 1994, to the month of March 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, at that point in time were you a member of the -- had you switched over to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you were appointed, were you a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The position of President of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what we're talking about. We're talking about that last position that you held. At what point did that position --

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed by the municipal assembly of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At whose recommendation, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The recommendation of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who in the SDS, sir? We want to be concrete and specific so we can get you back home to Bratunac hopefully by the end of the day. Who from the SDS made it a point to have you appointed to that position?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was nominated by the president of the Municipal Board, and that was Miroslav Deronjic. The municipal assembly accepted the nomination, and the delegates appointed me, that is, elected me. I did have a counter candidate. Two of us were nominated, and I won a larger number of votes and was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you're also Mr. Deronjic's neighbour; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our houses are perhaps ten metres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, who was the most powerful person in Bratunac during that period, you, Mr. Simic, or was there somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Deronjic who had the highest rating in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, in fact you know that he did have it; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could just please tell us exactly what your job entailed.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Executive Board is an executive body of the Assembly. In other terms, it's the local government, and I was at the head of that government, i.e., I was president of the Executive Board. The body had eight members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus your attention on July 1995, when Srebrenica fell. That would be 11 July 1995. Okay? So we're going to speak about that day.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you recall where you were on that day?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the building of the municipal assembly, in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you stay there the entire day?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence, Mr. Tesic, told me that he had received an order to mobilise members who had a wartime assignment and that I should go together with him out in the field to a location called Pribicevac. That location is about 25 kilometres away from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you go there?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you dressed in a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you were there, did you see Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tesic tell you to report to Colonel Blagojevic with these men that you were going there for?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you -- what did you do when you got to Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went ahead of Tesic to Pribicevac by about two hours. I was up there in a house which held the logistics section of the Bratunac Brigade. In that logistical unit, my son was also a member. I dropped by to see him, intending to wait for Tesic there, as well as the members of the labour brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed for about an hour, maybe an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did you see anyone while you were there?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please describe a little bit that experience.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I sat there inside that house talking to my son and the other young men who were in that room. Somebody says, "Here's General Mladic coming." I looked through the window and saw his car which was coming closer to the house. I went outside, and at that moment the vehicle carrying the general arrived. The general got out and asked me very sharply who I was and what I was doing there. I introduced myself, and he told me again very sharply to go away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you think he was going to do anything to you while you were leaving?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, considering the tone he used when he spoke to me, I was a bit frightened because I wasn't wearing my uniform. I wasn't carrying a weapon, and I thought to myself, I'd better go inside the house and pick up somebody's rifle and go back outside to show him that I wasn't out there for a picnic, which is what I did. And as I was coming out of the house, the general again intercepted me on the threshold because he was just coming in, and he said, "Are you still here? What are you waiting for? Get out of here. Go towards the command post." I made myself scarce, taking the path going through a valley towards the woods away from that logistical base, that house. Perhaps 200 or 300 metres on, I ran into Deronjic and the head of the police station, Josipovic. They asked me, "What are you doing?" And I answered, "I just had a very unpleasant encounter with the general," and they replied, "We are hiding from him too." The three of us stayed there for about 30 more minutes. In the meantime, Tesic caught up with me, and he took that labour unit to the command post where he handed them over to General Krstic. I did not go together with Tesic to the command post. Instead, I came back to the house that held the logistical unit because I had driven there alone. I took my car and drove back to my office in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you got back to Bratunac, did you attend any meetings later that day?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The next morning, did you -- which would be the day after Srebrenica fell, did you attend any meetings?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did. I was asked to come to the command of the Bratunac Brigade in the morning. I went there in the morning. I was sent to a room by the person on the gate. That room was on the ground floor to the right of the building, and I saw General Mladic in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you see Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had you been invited to go there by Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you alone or was anyone with you?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went there to the command alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed perhaps half an hour altogether there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While you were there during that half an hour, did anyone else show up?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After I arrived, Aco Tesic came, who was the head of the Secretariat for National Defence, and some two or three minutes later Ljubisav Simic, president of the municipal assembly arrived as well. Then again, after a certain brief period of time a local priest arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I understand he's still in Bratunac but no longer the priest. He left the priesthood; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was a caterer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you tell us a little bit about what happened during that half an hour that you were there on the ground floor of the Bratunac Brigade with General Mladic and the others.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, nothing special happened. The general greeted me and said, "I seldom see you in Srebrenica." I told him, "Well, General, I was discharging other duties and tasks." And then all of a sudden he asked me, "What are we to do with the Muslims in Srebrenica?" I replied to him, "We should see what they want. Perhaps it would be best to send them to Tuzla and Kladanj," since these two cities were closest at the time to the liberated Muslim territory, as they called it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you hear or were you able to hear what the others -- whether the others had a conversation with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he put the same questions to Tesic and Simic. I think that there were no other formal talks there following that. This didn't impress me as an official working meeting. It seemed more to be an invitation to meet the general. We were asked to come at 10.00 to the meeting at the Fontana Hotel. After that, I left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did all four of you -- were all four of you asked to go to the Hotel Fontana, that is you, Mr. Simic, Mr. Tesic, and the priest? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I think that he told only me and Simic about this. The other two were not invited, and they did not attend the meeting. They were not present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecution back on February 25, 1998, approximately, well, well over five -- five years ago. Incidentally, have you given any other statements other than that?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking since 1998, when you gave your statement to the Prosecution, February 25, did you give them any other statements? Did you meet with them, did you speak with them, or give them statements like you did back then, five years ago plus?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not meet representatives of the OTP after the February of 1998. However, I had contacts with Defence counsel for other accused, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the Prosecutor, but we'll talk about the other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. No, I -- I had only one meeting with the OTP representatives, and that was in February of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when was the first time that you were able to see your -- a copy of the statement that you gave to them some five years ago?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that for the first time three days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in looking at your statement, there's no mention of a meeting on the morning of the 12th of July, 1995, at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters on the first floor, between you, the others, and General Mladic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us, if you can, why this was not mentioned when you were being questioned by Mr. Ruez on 25 February 1998?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I considered that at the time not to be important. That meeting, or as some people call it a meeting at the command, did not really impress me as a typical meeting. I might have mentioned this earlier. This seemed more to be an opportunity to get together with the general and to receive an invitation to attend the meeting at 10.00 at the Fontana Hotel. That's why I never mentioned it before. I didn't consider it to be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's talk about the meeting at the Hotel Fontana. Could you please tell us from your recollection who attended the meeting there while you were there.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That meeting was attended by General Mladic, General Krstic, commander of the Dutch Battalion of UNPROFOR. I'm not positive, but I think his deputy was there as well because there were two men. Then there were representatives of the Muslims Ibro Nuhanovic, Nesim Mandic and a woman whose last name I don't know, but her first name is Camila. Representing the civilian government was President Simic, myself, and Mr. Deronjic. Chief of the public security station from Zvornik, Mr. Vasic, was there as well, and a colonel whose name I don't know and whose face was not familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before going to -- to hotel -- to this meeting at the Hotel Fontana, did you stop and pay a visit to Colonel Blagojevic and tell him you were going to this meeting or even just to say hello to him since you were in his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, nor did I see Colonel Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned the Muslim representatives. Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I knew Ibro Nuhanovic. I knew him really well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How is it that you knew him?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ibro Nuhanovic completed elementary school in Bratunac. After the elementary school, he attended the forestry secondary school in Ilidza. I also attended the first year of that school, and at the same time Nuhanovic was attending third year. Two or three months later, I transferred from the forestry school to the teacher's secondary school in Zvornik. Later on, I had encounters with Nuhanovic at work. He used to work at Sipad, which is a lumber processing company. He also worked in Bratunac for a while. We used to meet frequently, have a drink at the bar, and I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. During the meeting, did you have a speaking role? Did you speak?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to speak with your friend who was sitting on the other side representing the people in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the meeting was finished, once we got up from the table, Nuhanovic talked to the general and expressed concern whether things would unfold in the way it was stated at the meeting at that moment, I came up to Nuhanovic and shook hands with him, and I told him, "Ibro, trust the general."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And why did you say that to Mr. Nuhanovic, "Trust the general"?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to disperse any mistrust that he felt as to whether things would unfold in the way that was agreed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we speak about what was agreed at the meeting, have you had an opportunity to watch the video?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Four or five months ago, I quite by chance saw myself on television, in my house. I was writing something at the time and wasn't watching television carefully. I was basically just listening on and writing some of my stuff, and then all of a sudden I saw myself on the screen. I was surprised and perhaps even frightened a little bit, and I was wondering whether I was seeing things right, because I could see myself in the forefront of -- in the close-up at the screen, and I realised that that was a tape from the meeting. This was shown by the federal TV station in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So it wasn't shown to you back in 1998, and certainly none of the Defence lawyers have shown it to you?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to the best of your recollection, could you tell us, describe to us what you believe was said, was agreed upon at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, this meeting was chaired by General Mladic. He briefed everyone -- he briefed everyone on the Srebrenica operation, and the purpose of that was to see what would follow. The general proposed to the Muslim representatives to remain in the region and said that should they remain, they would have freedom of movement and freedom to live there, that that would be guaranteed. However, the Muslim side refused that very firmly. The woman called Camila spoke the most of all the Muslim representatives. She was very firm about the fact that the population wanted to leave the area. She was very emphatic about that. General suggested several more times to them that should they wish, they could remain in the area and be given all the guarantees. However, they were very clear that they didn't want that, that they wanted to go to Tuzla and Kladanj. Camila even asked the general about her daughters. I think that she had two daughters, 13 and 14-year-old. So she asked the general to place her daughters in the first transport and that she herself would remain for the last one. The general told her that if she had any anxiety over that that she could bring her daughters to the Fontana Hotel. She thanked the general for that offer and said that all she wanted was for her children to be placed on the first transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You told your friend, "Trust the general." Did you believe the general that nothing would happen to them, as you just described?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I had no doubts about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you think any harm would come to these people at any point?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It never even crossed my mind. I never thought that would happen. I thought that everything would be done in a proper way, as was agreed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, after the meeting, were you asked to do anything in particular and, if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: When it was clear -- when it became clear that people wanted to leave, we as representatives of the civilian government were tasked with working on the humanitarian side. We were asked to provide water and food for the people in Potocari. It was a very hot day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you do anything in particular, you yourself?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After we left the meeting, President Simic and I went to the municipal building, to my office, and there we drew up a plan of what needed to be done. We did in this in haste. We used two of our water tanks to take water to Potocari. These tanks belonged to the fire brigade. Then we also contacted the bakery asking that all bread existing and to be baked be distributed in Potocari. Our bakery is quite small. Therefore, President Simic went to Ljubovija, which is a neighbouring municipality in Serbia, six kilometres away, and he asked them to help us in this regard and to give whatever quantities of bread, juice, cookies, mineral water, and so on to us. We also contacted Zvornik, asking that they assist in providing bread and some other food items. Then we went to Potocari with the first batch of bread, and we encountered grave situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What did you see when you got to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I saw an enormous number of people. Potocari is a small place located between two hills, on the road between Bratunac and Srebrenica. In that entire area there were a lot of people, mostly the elderly, and then women, children, men of senior age. I also saw an UNPROFOR unit there which took up a position, so to speak, in order to -- to shield the people there in Potocari from people coming from elsewhere. It was a difficult situation, and I don't think I will ever forget this. I saw many familiar faces. There were people who recognised me. They called me by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you see -- now, did you do anything in particular while you were there?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was distributing bread, biscuits. I managed to pour water in containers. People recognised me, as I've said. A man who built my house before the war recognised me too. His name is Nijazija Jahic. He might have been 55 to 58 then. I didn't recognise him initially, and it wasn't until he approached me that I saw that it was him. He asked me whether I could help him and take him and his wife to the bus, enabling them to leave Potocari as soon as possible, which is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is he alive today?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is. He is alive. And about two years ago -- I think he lives in Central Bosnia now. I'm not sure whether the town is called Breza or Vares, but a Serb from that area who fled to Bratunac went there about two years ago, and then upon his return in Bratunac, he came to say me and he said, "Nijazija sends his greetings and his thanks. He is alive."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you do anything else while you were there, help anyone else onto any buses?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did. I recounted this part to the investigator when I spoke to him in 1998. I was recognised by a man named Muhamed. I knew him too. He was originally from the Glogova village, and before the war he used to work in the municipal assembly as a messenger, as a gofer. He asked me for permission to put his uncle on the bus. The uncle was in a wheelchair and couldn't move on his own. I said, "Where is the uncle?" And he showed me to a place 30 or 40 metres away. When we got to the man, I saw another -- another group of people, disabled people in wheelchairs. I said it would be a good idea to take them all ahead of the line and put them on the bus. At a distance of about 150 metres down the road leading to Bratunac I saw General Mladic, and I thought to myself that I would go to the general and tell him about those disabled people, which I did. I came up to the general and said there were about 30 disabled persons in wheelchairs who needed to be escorted onto the bus, and he said, "Go ahead, do it." I went back to Muhamed and said, "All of you now head for the buses." The buses were about 200 metres away down. And he said, "My friends are all away. Who is going to push the wheelchairs?" It was the kind of wheelchair that you had to push. He said, "Wait for a while while I get them." And it took about 20 minutes before they got organised, and then I took them ahead of the queue, and they were put on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. A couple of questions. One, on that incident, one -- when you were doing that, were you trying to ethnically cleanse the area? Was that the purpose for doing that, to forcibly remove those people from that area, or was this an act of -- an humanitarian act?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ethnic cleansing never occurred to me. It never occurred to me that I was ethnically cleansing anyone while I was doing that. My only thought was how to help those people. Those were very difficult moments. We're talking about very old people here. There was a moment when I thought, What if my parents were in the same situation? You can believe me when I say that I did my best. I did everything I could to help them to the extent of my physical and other abilities. There was no question of ethnic cleansing. It never crossed my mind, and it never seemed to me that there could be anyone who would see it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, why did you have -- why did you go up to General Mladic to ask permission to see if they could get on the buses?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I could not explain it now why I went to see him. I didn't have to. I certainly didn't need his permission for that, but I reckoned to myself that maybe I had better go up to him and inform him that I would do that. Not because I needed his permission or because I thought that he would not allow it, I just thought it was better to tell him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how long were you in Potocari that day?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Two and a half, maybe three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what did you do after that? I should say where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's very probable that I went home for about an hour to have lunch to refresh myself before I went back to the municipal building, to my office, because the job of providing people with water and food wasn't finished. We had to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And later on, do you recall what you did?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: At what time? You mean in the afternoon? That afternoon and evening was spent doing the same activities. That evening I went out to town, and the rest of the time I was mainly in my office. Those were rare moments when I was alone in my office. There was always someone around. The evening found me in my office, and I was receiving a visit of the director of the utilities enterprise, Dragan Mirkovic. We were talking in my office. I believe Simic was receiving some foreigners at the time. He was not in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Incidentally, where is your office in relation to Mr. Simic's office?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: We used the same entrance. Before you get to my office there is a smaller office where the secretary sits. My office is on the right-hand side. Simic's is on the left. But we used the same entrance to the waiting-room. My office is on the right. Simic's is on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, about what time in the evening did this gentleman show up? Mirkovic, was it?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He was in my office for quite awhile. It was already 9.00 p.m., and we were still sitting there. But much earlier, around 7.00 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, while you were there in your office with Mr. Mirkovic, did you notice anything unusual?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed looking out of the window that three buses had arrived, because the municipal building is facing the street and there were three buses downstairs. I noticed they were full. Mirkovic and I then got out of my office, and as we were coming out of the municipal building we saw a bus parked right outside. There were many people standing. There were many people inside the bus and one policeman standing outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you recognise the policeman that was standing outside guarding the bus?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I had never see him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say a policeman, was that a military policeman or a civilian policeman?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Those were civilian policemen wearing their usual blue police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, while you were out there seeing those buses what, if anything, did you do?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Standing there by the buses, I saw that inside the bus a man who was standing in the middle of the bus was knocking on the window. I came closer and recognised the man who was knocking. It was Omo Jahic from the Bljecevo village who used to work in the mine before the war. He was also a deputy to the municipal assembly, and I knew him. I said to the policeman, "This man in there wants to tell me something. May I go in?" And the policeman gave me his permission. I got onto the bus, took the seat next to the driver, and said, "Omo, what do you want?" And he said, "Buco, brother, can you give me some water?" I looked out the door and said to the policeman, "Can I give this man some water?" And he said, "Yes." He was holding a large jerrycan of five litres. I passed it on, and when the others in the bus saw it they all raised their small jerrycans, and we served everybody on the bus. Since there were bathrooms on the ground floor we filled jerrycans with water and passed them on inside the buses. We did the same with the second bus, and we certainly passed certainly no less than 50 jerrycans of water. It was a terribly hot, scorching night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else that night while you were there?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That night I ran into Deronjic in the street, because I had seen other buses in the other part of the town closer to Jeliste, and I asked Deronjic, "What's going on here?" And he was very sharp when he replied. He said we were being set up by the people from Milici. They are sending these people. And he mentioned Rajko Dukic. He was very angry and indignant about this too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: Who is Rajko Dukic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Rajko Dukic is a man from Milici, director of the bauxite mine and the number one man in Milici. Deronjic's counterpart in Milici. He held the same position. In fact, what Deronjic meant for Bratunac, he meant for Milici. Perhaps even had more importance. Anyway, Deronjic was very angry and very upset that these people were being sent over to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So from that conversation, at least you got the impression that Mr. Deronjic thought that these buses had come from Milici and had been sent by his counterpart in Milici, Mr. Dukic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did -- did he express -- other than expressing anger, did Mr. Deronjic ask you or order you or request that you contact Mr. Blagojevic, perhaps, to see what he could do to get these buses out of Bratunac that came from Milici?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. On the contrary. I told Deronjic, "Commander Deronjic, work your own lines of communication to inform somebody upstairs and ask them what's going on." I thought that he was higher up and he was better connected with the political leadership and probably the military leadership too. I did not mention Colonel Blagojevic at all either in the sense that he should inform him or that he should ask him to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now you -- how many -- how many of these police officers were guarding each bus? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very few. I don't even think that each bus had its own policeman guarding it. In my estimate, I think there was one policeman for every two buses. In my opinion, very few people were -- very few men were providing security for the buses. At one point I saw a driver standing outside a municipal building, and I saw only two policemen guarding three buses, the three buses that is were outside the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In light of the time, Your Honour, if we could break here and we'll pick up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have 30 minutes' break. We'll resume at ten minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. And how long do you think your direct examination will last?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, hopefully we will finish before this session. I think maybe an hour, maybe less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Maybe less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there a problem though?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. I just want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, we were speaking about the evening of July 12, 1995, when you were out there on the streets of Bratunac and you saw the buses that you believed, after having spoken with Mr. Deronjic, had come from Milici; right? I'm going to pick up from there.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, right before we left off, you indicated that they -- there was one guard perhaps for one or two buses, one police officer for one or two buses. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did that concern you at that point in time, that here were these buses full of Muslim men inside the town of Bratunac, guarded by one or two people per bus?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That made my quite anxious, because I thought there were very few police guarding the buses, and we had also received a notification that out there at the playground the Muslim men were calling out to each other and communicating. That caused additional concern, that they might get out of the buses. And there were very few guards at the playground too. So we sent some retired people from among the residents who had their own weapons to go to the playground and create an impression that there were enough guards. And the bus drivers, in order to stop this communication and the shouting, turned on the engines of the buses so that the noise would prevent people from calling out to each other and shouting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that you -- you asked some retired residents to go there so that there would be a make-believe image that the buses were guarded heavily, I guess. Is there any reason why you or Mr. Deronjic did not suggest to go to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters and demand or request the brigade commander to bring his soldiers into town to guard the buses?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we did not go to the command because we knew that there was practically no one at that command. All the troops were out in the field, on the front, together with the commanders. So we did not ask for any assistance from the army. We contacted instead the head of the police station, Mr. Josipovic, asking him for assistance in terms of providing his own men as guards, but he was not able to help out much. In addition to the retired persons, however, we also engaged some very young boys, aged 15, 16, 17, to go to the playground and create the impression that the security was beefed up, because there were no able-bodied men in town, in Bratunac. There were only women, children, and the elderly. Everyone else was already engaged on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To your knowledge or from your observations was any food provided to those folks that were in the buses?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing, there was no organised, continuous supply. Something was occasionally sporadically provided to individual people or groups. If somebody knew someone, then they would get some food or water to them, but there was no organised supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, anything else unusual that night, before we move on to the next morning which would be two days after the fall of Srebrenica, July 13, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't -- I can't think of anything important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, let's talk about the next day, the following morning. How did that start?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That, the 13th. This is --

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The 13th, yes. In the course of the night, those buses left Bratunac. They vanished before the morning. I only observed that individual persons were brought to the school building not far from the municipality building, about a hundred metres away from the municipal building. Two, three, or five persons at a time would be tank out of a bus and brought to the school building. Since I knew the local policemen, I asked them, "Who are these people? What are you doing with them?" And they answered, "Those are men who were captured or had surrendered up there on the road." And maybe some Muslim men simply wandered into Bratunac by mistake and were brought in, taken into custody to the school building. That answer was enough for me. And I think after that, I went up there to the command to see the assistant for logistics, Mr. Trisic, Dragoslav Trisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Before we talk about that, when you had this conversation with the police officer, did you ask him who authorised for these people to come to Bratunac and to be detained in buildings that would appear to be property of the Bratunac municipality? Did you ask him that question?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. But nobody in the municipal government was asked to put the school building at their disposal for that purpose. There are two primary schools in Bratunac. The primary school to which people were brought and where they were detained was not operating as a school at the time because it had been destroyed in 1992 and was not fit for teaching purposes. We have another primary school building which was serving as a school. So that from 1992, from July 1992 to July 1995, that other primary school was standing empty, demolished, with no windows. And I don't know anything about the reasons why those people were brought there and detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me go back and ask my question. Did you ask the police officer or anyone else who authorised, who ordered that those men be brought there?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask, and I don't know who ordered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that you went after that to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters and you met with Mr. Trisic, the assistant commander for rear services; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was the reason for having -- for going there and meeting with Mr. Trisic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the command base to see Mr. Trisic because he was the person at the command who was in charge with liaison with the municipality. Generally speaking, our contacts with the brigade went between the commander and the local government, and the commander transferred most of that job to his assistant because the -- the activities covered by the Executive Board fell within the purview on their side of the logistics unit. So I went to see that man to collect some information and see what the situation was on the front line. Apart from being assistant for logistics, Trisic was a former schoolmate of mine, a good friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday we talked -- during your period -- during that period when the Bratunac Brigade had been formed, do you know how many commanders had come and gone approximately?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know that many commanders came and went, but from the time when I took up my position in the municipality - that was in October, October 1994 - there were two commanders. The one who was commander at the time when I took up my post in the municipality was Ognjenovic, and just before the Srebrenica operation started, he was replaced by Commander Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the assistant commander for rear services? How many had come and gone during the period that you had dealings with the Bratunac Brigade in your official capacity?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was one and only assistant commander for logistics from 1992 to 1995 and that was Dragoslav Trisic. He did not change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you -- how long did you stay with Mr. Trisic that morning?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the time I came into his office perhaps 20 minutes passed before I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Anything in particular -- was anything in particular discussed during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: He told me briefly what was going on on the front line, nothing in particular, but he said one thing, "Do you know who was captured and was being held in detention here?" And I said, "I don't know." And he said "Resid Sinanovic. He's now in the detention of the military police."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what else?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I said to Dragan Trisic, "Dragan, I would like to see Resid if possible. Where is he exactly?" He said to me, "He's down there with the military police in the custody of Zlatan Calanovic." And I said, "What do you think? Should we go and see him? Could that be done?" Trisic said, "I will not go." I said to Trisic, "I would like to see Resid," because Resid is a man with whom I worked from 1980 to 1994 at the police. He was my chief, and I was his deputy. In addition to that, Resid and I were close friends. We were friends even before I started working for the police and on finishing my term with the police, we continued socialising. We were very good friends, family friends. This is why I expressed my desire to go and see Resid. Trisic said to me, "Here's the phone number. Call Zlatan Calanovic and go and ask him if you can see Resid." I took the number. As soon as I also knew Zlatan Calanovic, we were acquaintances, I called him up and I asked him, "Zlatan, can I see Resid," to which he replied, "Sure, why not." I asked when I could come, and he said, "Right away." I said, "I'll come now, then." Zlatan Calanovic and the detention unit where Resid was held was 30 to 40 metres from the command. I offered to Trisic to come along with me and he refused, and then I said to him, "All right. I'll go by myself." I went to Zlatan's. I saw him in his office. I sat there, and he went to get Resid from the place where he was detained. He probably didn't say to Resid that I was waiting for him in Zlatan's office. I concluded that based on the expression on Resid's face when he entered into the office and saw me there. I got up, extended my hand to him. We shook hands. He clinched my hand, and we stayed there for quite awhile. He pulled me to him and kissed me. I felt uncomfortable. I thought that he was expecting me to help him, and I told him right away that I wouldn't be able to help him then, and I didn't consider that I should, that I need to help him, because I believed that Resid would be treated in accordance with the laws governing the treatment of prisoners of war. Therefore, I thought that he would be either exchanged or something else. Therefore, I told him that I worked at the -- that I worked with the municipal government, that this was a military operation, and he said to me, "Yes, I know. I heard when I came to the municipality. We heard it on the radio. It was announced on the radio. I do not expect any help from you now. I'm simply grateful that you came to see me and to talk to me." We sat there. Zlatan went out, and we stayed there for an hour, perhaps a bit more, talking. There were no visible traces on Resid. I asked him whether somebody abused him, whether he was hungry. He said, "No, I'm not hungry. Nobody beat me. Nobody harassed me." So we stayed together for an hour, and when we parted -- or, rather, Zlatan Calanovic came back somewhat later. Since both of them were lawyers, they exchanged a few words. All three of us were avid anglers, and we talked about fishing as well. In the end, Zlatan and I gave a packet of cigarettes each to Resid. We said goodbye, and that was our last meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you know what happened to this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: His brother called me, his middle brother, Zihnija who used to be a JNA officer before the war, a captain serving in Skopje. Maybe some six months after July he asked me if I knew of Resid's fate. He called me from Skopje. I don't know how he got my telephone number. And he asked me this and I told him I had seen Resid and I believe that he had gone to Tuzla or Kladanj. He told me that was not the case and that Resid was missing. I know that Resid's wife was in Germany, that she went there sometime in 1992 or 1993 on the UNHCR truck. He sent his wife and children to Germany. So then I asked him perhaps Resid is in Germany with his family, and he said, "No, no. I talk to his wife almost every night, but he's not there." He had some information that some of the Muslim prisoners were sent to work in the mines in Serbia, and he was wondering whether Resid was there. I told him, "Zihnija, I know nothing about that. I don't think that's the case." And he asked me to verify this information through my channels. After that, he didn't call me again. He called me perhaps five months ago. He's in Sarajevo now working for the state border service. He called me to get some certificates for Resid in the municipality, birth certificates or marriage certificates, because his wife needed that to get something settled regarding the apartment. However, Resid is gone, to my regret.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, this is the 13th. Is there anything else of significance on that day that we need to discuss before we move on to the next day?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that anything important happened that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So nothing that you recollect significant after you left the Bratunac Brigade, after your visit? If you don't recollect, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So let's move on to the 14th, 14th of July, the next day. Do you recall anything unusual happening that particular day? Does anything stick out in your mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, this question is too broad. It seems to me a fishing expedition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, it's not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to lead --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can lead, I can lead. I don't want any objections. I did that yesterday; I drew an objection on a preparatory question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you? I think Mr. McCloskey is very cooperative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The morning of July 14th, sir. Could you please explain to us what happened, if anything?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the morning hours - it could have been at around 10.00 - the secretary of the SDS called me asking me to come up to the party offices right away. I went there. These offices are perhaps 200 metres from the municipal building. I entered the office where the secretary sat, and there by the coffee table was a man in a uniform, and I could tell that he was a colonel. The man was not familiar to me. That was the first time I saw him. The SDS offices consist of two rooms, and from that office where the secretary was, one enters into the other room which is behind the door. So this colonel introduced himself, said that he was Colonel Dana [as interpreted]. He offered --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was his name again? Who was the Colonel?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The name was Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: He asked me to sit down, and he talked to me for about ten minutes unofficially, as if we were acquaintances. He offered me a drink. I accepted it. And after that, he suggested that we go to the other office, the neighbouring office, because there was some people there to wanted to talk to me. I opened the door, entered the adjacent office, and I saw two officers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for one second. I want to go step-by-step. You're at the SDS office; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're in the first room as you walk in.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you just indicated that Colonel Beara offered you a drink. That's the SDS office. How could he be off -- how could he --

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, in that first room, the first office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If he's in that office and that's not his office, how could he be offering you a drink?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how he had that drink, but there was a bottle on the coffee table in front of him. He offered me a drink. It wasn't the secretary who offered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So there was a bottle right there, and he -- okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you went into the other room, who did you see?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I saw two officers there. One is lieutenant colonel, the other one was colonel. I did not know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did they give you their names?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you walked in did Colonel Beara stay behind drinking or did he also come into the room as well?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: He remained in the first office. I went into the other room by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So what happened when you walked in and you saw the colonel and lieutenant colonel?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I greeted them. I extended my hand, and almost immediately they asked me what we had in terms of construction machines. I told them that at the brick factory we had a machine called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name of the machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please stop. You need to speak slowly and clearly. So what was the name the machine or what kind of machine? Describe it.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The machine was called Ult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ult?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Ult. U-l-t, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: They asked whether we could put it at their disposal, and I said yes. I had some assumptions as to why they were asking this machine from us. I thought they might need it to dig trenches, to continue their military operations at the front line. However, there had already been an incident in Kravica in the premises of the co-op --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. We're going to go step-by-step. So you now mention there was an incident in Kravica. This is the morning of the 14th. When did you hear about this incident?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about it just before going to the office. Two men came or, rather, two directors of co-ops came to see me. The first one was Jovan Nikolic, and Dragan Nikolic was the director of the co-op in Kravica they came and told me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So when they asked you for the Ult, one of your assumptions was that they might need it for that incident. Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were my guesses. They didn't tell me why they needed it, but I thought that it was either for military operations, for digging trenches. I did not ask them why they needed the machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So what happened?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, thinking that they might also need it to bury people, I remembered Djurkovic who was the operator of the machine, because I heard that in 1992, he was involved in it and felt badly ever since. I wanted to protect the man from possibly getting involved in it again, so I told the officers that they could have the machine but not the operator because he wasn't really suitable for that, to which one of them sharply and perhaps even rudely asked me, "Is it really your job to decide who will be operating the machine and who will not?" I said, "I apologise. This was just a comment of mine."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you frightened at all of these two men or... ?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't afraid of them, but the tone that he used didn't make me frightened but made me realise that I should not get into the discussion with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, this incident, this encounter at the SDS office on July 14th and the conversation with these two officers with respect to the Ult was not mentioned by you five years ago when you gave your statement to members of the Office of the Prosecution; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but I didn't think at the time that it was very important and that I needed to mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, why didn't you think it was important?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I thought that the Ult machine would be used by the army for military operations. These were just my guesses. Nobody told me what the machines would actually be used for, so that's why I believed at the time that it wasn't that important, that I didn't need to mention it to investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Since then and as you -- as you are here today, have you heard what happened to the men, the Muslim men that were detained, captured, separated? Have you heard what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Lack of foundation. There's only the suggestion of a few men in this person's knowledge that even had been detained. So a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's a ridiculous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I could not understand you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Under this person's testimony thus far, he has not established but yet just a very few people. Mr. Resid has been detained. A few people on buses, but he said they got shipped out to Kladanj. So I -- the thousands of people that we all know about have not been a part of the discussion but they were part of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karnavas, could you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me, for the purposes of speeding the process up and since we've already covered this, I'll ask some leading background questions. You indicated that you saw men in buses on the night of the 12th; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You indicated that you saw men in the school building that wasn't used at the time. I believe it's called Vuk Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You learned that there were men in the stadium; correct? And you saw that as well?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, from the Kravica incident, did you ever learn approximately how many people were killed in that incident?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where these people were from, the ones who had been brought to Kravica. I didn't see those people. However, I heard that between 7 to 800 people had been taken there. Jovan Nikolic told me this, as did Dragan Nikolic when they came on the 14th to the municipal building to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, again today is 19 -- 2004. The Prosecution spoke to you five years plus and never in between. Since that period of time, as you stand here today, have you heard approximately how many people went missing as a result of the events after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that. It was announced in the media as well. I heard the figure, and it ranges from 5 to 6 to even 8.000 people who went missing in the Srebrenica operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you heard that in the media, did you believe it?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, the figure seems high. Whether I believe it or not, I can't be specific about that. What is certain is that a lot of people perished, a lot of people. Perhaps as many as the number indicated, but a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I heard various stories, how a lot of corpses were found in the forests on the road from Srebrenica to Tuzla. Also in Kravica. I heard that there were such incidents in Zvornik municipality as well. I think that Pilica was mentioned and some other locations. Therefore, I think that there were a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you hear of any burial operations, a cover-up effort to cover up these atrocities?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have. I heard about that. I heard about the attempt to move the mass graves such as, for example, from Glogova to Srebrenica municipality. I don't know the exact sites, but I know the names of the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were questioned -- you were questioned back in 1998 about burials, and I believe Glogova was one of the areas that -- where there had been some discussion between you and Mr. Ruez. Do you remember reading that when you just saw your statement the other day?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know exactly what the investigator was asking me about then. I didn't know whether he meant Serb gravesites or the Muslim ones. I didn't think that he asked me about the Muslim gravesites but that he asked me about the gravesites in general, which was part of my duties at the municipality. We had to provide coffins for funerals, and we organised a lot of mass funerals in one day. We would have 50 or 40 people buried in one day. So I spent a lot of my time at work in taking care of this, because the municipality had to provide everything, including the coffins. So I thought that the investigator was interested in that and not in this other matter. This is why I mentioned Glogova. I said that Serbs had not been buried there, that it was a Muslim village, and that the Serbs were buried in other cemeteries, in Bratunac and so on, and this is why I didn't answer his question about these gravesites that had been moved. I did not take part in Muslim funerals, only in the funerals of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, how far is Kravica, not the warehouse, but Kravica from Glogova?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps five kilometres. Four to five.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And was there an incident that occurred there where a lot of Serbs were slaughtered by the Muslim forces, Naser Oric's folks?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were incidents in Kravica during Christmas of 1993. Also in December of 1992 in Bjelovac where 109 people were killed in one day. That was the funeral at which the most people were buried in one day. There were also incidents in the village of Fakovici, Zagoni. In each of these cases, about 30 Serbs were killed, mostly civilians and fewer military servicemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Is it possible, sir, that you might have been confused when talking to Mr. Ruez was talking to you about Glogova and Serbs, and you thought that it was Serbs being buried as a result of the 150, I believe, Serbs that were slaughtered by Naser Oric's soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the investigator must not have been very decisive or clear when he was asking questions, because I thought he was speaking about Serb funerals. And then he said, "No, I'm not asking you about Serb funerals. I'm talking about the burials and funerals of Muslims." And if he had said so from the start, I certainly wouldn't have been telling him about Serb funerals. Why would any Serb funerals take place in Glogova, a Muslim village? I think that the investigator was definitely not very clear there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- but while you were describing the incident in Kravica, you referred to the Muslims as Turks. Do you recall reading that in your statement, when you said the Turks did such-and-such?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how my tongue slipped. It just came out. I blurted it out because it was the jargon in my community at the time. People referred to them as Turks. They called us Vlasi and Chetniks, and it must have somehow slipped across my tongue, because I don't understand to this day how it could have -- how it could have happened that I referred to them in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I just have a couple of more areas. First of all, Mr. Borovcanin? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How is it that you know him?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I met Mr. Borovcanin in 1992. He came into Bratunac from Kladanj and he was commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During those days did you have any contact with him, Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was in touch with Mr. Borovcanin and we were good friends because my wife also worked with the police. That was another connection between us. Later, Borovcanin was transferred to Bijeljina, and he was promoted into a general of the police force. There was a ceremony, a promotion ceremony at Bratunac for him that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During those days, July 12th, 13th, 14th, did you come into contact with Mr. Borovcanin? That's my concrete question.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did have one encounter with Mr. Borovcanin. It could have been the 11th or the 12th. I'm not quite sure. Since his logistical base was on the premises of the Lovac restaurant in Bratunac, he came to me and said that his unit had run out of food, and he asked me if I had any tinned food in stock.
