I called up my staff and asked if we had any to spare and then replied to Borovcanin that we could spare 1.000 tins. He promised to refund us when he gets his own supplies, but that never happened. It doesn't matter. In any case, we gave him 1.000 cans of food. That was my only encounter with him regarding this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you saw him, did he tell you that he had been -- did he mention if he had been seconded to and was working under or subordinated to General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't, and I did not broach the subject myself, and I didn't ask him anything, nor was I really interested in that hierarchy. I was aware that he was in charge of a special unit, but who was above and who was below him, I didn't really want to know, and he didn't volunteer any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During those days that we've discussed, did you come into contact with Mr. Blagojevic at all, 12th -- we've talked about the 11th, 12th, 13th or thereafter. During those critical days, did you come into contact with Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of the Srebrenica operation, I never ran into Blagojevic and never had any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, over the years, since -- now we're closing in close to ten years now, it's nine plus -- or nine, did you ever hear from anyone or come across any documents that would lead you to believe that Colonel Blagojevic was directly or indirectly involved in any of the activities, any of these atrocities?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I mean, really. I never heard from anyone that Colonel Blagojevic was involved in any atrocities regarding Srebrenica. You said yourself that more than ten years have elapsed. The mere fact that Blagojevic was arrested caused a great uproar in Bratunac, and disbelief, because Blagojevic is known in Bratunac as a good officer, a good person, a man who has understanding for everyone, who is willing to help everyone, and who wouldn't harm anyone. I never heard from anyone that he was involved in anything bad. What you can most often hear in Bratunac is that he is a man who found himself in the wrong place at the wrong time. I don't know if I put it right, but he really didn't have anything to do with anything there, and it just so happened that he was named commander of that unit in Bratunac at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. One final question. Before Mr. Blagojevic, we had another commander that you had some contact with, and that was Mr. Ognjenovic; correct? I'm pronouncing --

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean Ognjenovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, when I came to work for the municipal government in October 1994, I continued the work related to logistical support for the brigade, and in my recollection -- rather, I don't have a good memory of Commander Ognjenovic. He constantly put pressure on us. I had the impression that he was not particularly fond of the civilian authorities. He constantly came up with some demands that we were not able to meet. He seemed to have a mania of grandeur in those demands. Give us new uniforms. Give us more food and better food. And I -- we kept telling him, "We don't have the resources. The enterprises are not working at full capacity. You must understand." And whenever we asked him to do something for us, to release from his troops some people who were needed in the labour force to improve the production of food, to give the army more cigarettes, he would not relieve the soldiers. How would we then be able to go halfway to meet his requests? And I also had the impression that he was not particularly liked among his troops. He was arrogant in his treatment of his own soldiers, and they had no love lost for him either. That was my impression of these two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With that -- with that background, do you know whether he had some sort of policy that he was implementing which was perhaps why he was asking you for all of these resources, to make the life miserable and unbearable for the folks in Srebrenica so they would be ethnically cleansed from the area? Did he ever express this policy to you?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that he was more intent on making our life difficult than the life of Muslims. He was so insistent in his demands. But I don't think he was doing anything in particular to make life impossible for the Muslims. I think he was making trouble more for the civilian authorities. I don't know if I was clear enough. He spent more time squeezing us and putting pressure. I cannot find the right words for -- to describe his attitude towards us, but he was a very unpleasant man and very difficult to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I failed to mention earlier or to ask you, was this some sort of a process to take care of the abandoned property of those who had left the area? So Muslim leaving the Bratunac area, going someplace else and then a Serb coming in to occupy that premises? Was there some sort of a process? Could you please explain that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the times of war operations, a lot of Serb refugees came to Bratunac, people from Central Bosnia, from Zenica, from other towns, and even people who were affected by war operations in Croatia, from the Knin area, came to our town. We have some records saying -- showing that refugees from 66 municipalities of the former Yugoslavia came to Bratunac. We put them up into vacated Serbian and Muslim properties, and we did so in keeping with a government decision on the accommodation of displaced persons and refugees. In other words, we allocated properties to these people for temporary use, temporary use. That was the term, meaning until the return of rightful owners. I don't know if I put this clearly enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think you have.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just one more thing. In our municipal government, we had a special service in charge of these affairs, and I think there is one person that would tell you more about this much, that's Zlatan Calanovic. He headed at the time the service in charge of everything that had to do with allocation of property to refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Davidovic. I have no further questions for you. However, Mr. Stojanovic and Mr. McCloskey, the Prosecutor, may have some questions as well as the Judges. I hope you can be as honest and complete with your answers as you have been with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask a couple of questions, but I don't know whether it is a good idea for me to start now or maybe wait until after the break. I don't think my questioning would take more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we still have a few minutes left in this session, and we don't see that the testimony of this witness is somehow related to your client. Try to make your questions as simple as possible so that we can finish it in five or six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that you served as President of the Executive Board of the Bratunac municipality from October 1994 to 1997.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, as President of the Executive Board, you supervised public enterprises in your municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that the utilities enterprise is one of the public enterprises in the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this connection, I want to ask you one thing. You said that that evening, on the 12th, in the evening, you talked to Dragan Mirkovic. Which post did he occupy then?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was director of the utilities enterprise, public utilities enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the utilities enterprise have any machinery at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: They did have a small excavator called Skip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this connection, I want to ask you -- what would be the procedure to follow it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- well -- yes, please continue, but you have to bear in mind that the interpreters have a hard time to catch up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to slow down because we are speaking the same language.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, what would be the procedure to follow if the army needs to use that Skip machine or any other asset of a public utilities enterprise?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think there are several ways for the army to get it. They can get it directly from the utilities enterprise. They can go through the Executive Board, and they can also go through the local Secretariat for National Defence, which secretariat would requisition the asset in question. Those are three procedural possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago a relevant case where you met with two officers you didn't know. Would I be right in saying that they did not belong to the Bratunac Brigade, because you didn't know them?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So these officers came along from somewhere outside, and they wanted to requisition this machine from the brickworks specifically. Would it be possible to bypass the regular requisitioning procedure and take that machine without going through the Bratunac Brigade? Would these officers be able to requisition the machine without ever contacting the Bratunac Brigade and without following the procedure?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Do you mean to say whether it could be requisitioned without consulting the Executive Board and without taking a decision on the requisitioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would say everything is possible in war. Bratunac is a small place. Many people -- in fact everyone knows everyone else, and it's possible to do things without strictly following the procedure. Would that answer satisfy you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I take your reply to mean yes, it was possible for these officers to requisition the asset, the machine, from the enterprise, directly from the utilities enterprise without following the procedure, without going through the Bratunac Brigade or the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they had to have contacts with somebody from the enterprise. Maybe they could get somebody from the Executive Board to give a call to the utilities enterprise, or maybe they could get somebody from the national defence secretariat to get them to instruct the enterprise to allocate this machine. Yes, it's possible. But one possibility is certain, the possibility that the procedure is not followed and that personal connections are used instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So it's possible that this machine could have been requisitioned without any steps being taken through or by the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible. Everything is possible in wartime. That is my belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more clarification. You said today at one point, "Burials were part of my job in the municipal government. We had a lot of mass funerals, and that was the job of the municipal government to provide for the organisation of funerals and supply of coffins."

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have other activities in your purview in cooperation with the civilian defence force regarding the mopping up of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: With the civilian defence, concerning the mopping up of the terrain. I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to put it in simpler terms. At that time, that means in 1995, did you have a municipal headquarters of civilian defence?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it one of the jobs, one of the tasks of the civilian defence headquarters to mop up the terrain, to cleanse, to clean up the terrain, to clean up the terrain by collecting corpses of people, animals after battles, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the municipality was involved in such tasks. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that the civilian defence was subordinated to the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In a way, yes, but it was also subordinated to the national defence secretariat. It was their body, but it was also subordinated to the Executive Board. However, the Executive Board issued such orders very rarely indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those assignments were allocated, as a rule, through the national defence secretariat, that is its section in Bratunac. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was intrigued by something I heard during the questioning. It was a question recorded in the transcript under number 525120235, and I would like a clarification. I think it is a very dangerous error if it is an error. 525120235. That is the line in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Since we were going to be taking our break I already asked that those pages be printed out so that I would examine them carefully, because I picked it up just as Mr. Blagojevic has picked it up. Then I thought I would clean it up or clarify it on redirect, but I concur with Mr. Blagojevic. He's actually correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. I think it's time for a break. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, did you check with the transcript during the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I do have the transcript and I am, at the appropriate time, ready to ask some questions that would clarify the issue, but I can wait until Mr. McCloskey's cross-examination, and after, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I will give you the opportunity after the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I ask that that happen first, Your Honour, so we don't into this back and forth? I have no objection if there is something significant that needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm ready, Your Honour, and I think that's a fair request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you were asked earlier by Mr. Stojanovic about the procedure that needs to be followed, and it was -- the question dealt with the Skip, the Skip machine or any other public asset of a public enterprise. Do you recall being asked that question?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That is your answer. I'll read it back to you and we'll analyse t it will take a couple of minutes. You indicated and I'm reading from the transcript, this would be -- read these transcripts, but it's 115016, and I think it's on page 49. You state: "I think there are several ways for the army to get it. They can get it directly from the utilities enterprise. They can go through the Executive Board, and they can also go through the local Secretariat for National Defence, which secretariat -- which requisition the asset in question. Those are three procedural possibilities." Do you recall being asked that question and giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It was then asked of you whether the gentleman, the colonel and the lieutenant colonel that had been making these demands of you on the morning of July 14, 1995, whether they were from the Bratunac Brigade, and you indicated that they were not; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just for the record, Colonel Blagojevic wasn't there either, was he?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nor did they ever say at any time that they were there on behalf of Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the next question which needs a little bit of clarification. You say so -- the question is: "So these officers came along from somewhere outside, and they wanted to requisition this machine from the brickworks specifically." And then the question is: "Would it be possible to bypass the regular requisitioning procedure and take that machine without going through the Bratunac Brigade? Would these officers be able to requisition the machine without ever contacting the Bratunac Brigade and without following the procedure?" And at that point, your answer was: "I don't understand the question. Do you mean to say whether it would being requisitioned without consulting the Executive Board and without taking a decision on the requisitioning," and so on. Now, first of all, first of all, in your previous answer where you said that there are three possible ways, directly, the army directly can go. They can go to the Executive Board, or they go to the local Secretariat for National Defence. Nowhere in your answer are you suggesting that they had -- that these officers had to go through the Bratunac Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They didn't ask for that through the Bratunac Brigade. They asked for that personally, and I saw them for the first time then. The common procedure was to go through the commander of the brigade to the local authorities or perhaps to the assistant for logistics who would then implement it. I think that was the usual procedure. This request did not go through the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether these would be -- these folks were from the Main Staff or the corps or from someplace else?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I could only speculate, because I'd never seen these people before. Their faces were not familiar to me let alone their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if they were from the corps, from the Drina Corps, would not the procedure be that they would have to go to the Zvornik district Ministry of National Defence and place the requisition through them? And if you don't know the answer, that's fine. We'll have the appropriate witness who can answer all of these questions.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was unusual that they contacted me directly and requested this from me. However, at the time I didn't pay much attention to this. Let me just tell you what was the procedure that followed. I called on the phone the brickworks director, Nikolic, and I told him the people from the army will come. Give them the machine. He said, "I have no fuel." I said, "They will give you the fuel and if there are any problems, give me a call." I don't know what happened next with the machine. I don't know whether they took the machine or not; I simply informed the director that these people would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you ever assume at that point in time that these two officers had gone to the brigade, had contacted Colonel Blagojevic and they had gotten his permission to come there, these higher ranking officers, or from a higher echelon I should say, get the permission from Blagojevic to come to you to make the requisition? Did you ever form that assumption based on what was going on in that office at that morning?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't make any further assumptions. I simply didn't analyse this any more. I conveyed this to the brickworks director, and I don't know what happened next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you never contacted Colonel Blagojevic or anyone in the Bratunac Brigade to see whether these two gentlemen, a colonel and a lieutenant colonel with Colonel Beara who was drinking outside, had been sent there by Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know who sent them. I did not inquire into this. I didn't see Blagojevic there, nor was his name mentioned in any context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one final question. At the time when you met Colonel Beara, when you walked into the SDS office, he was sitting there and I believe there was a bottle of whisky where he was drinking that morning, did you know that man? Did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first time I saw him. He told me what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you know his significance in the Main Staff -- or in the VRS, I should say.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, not from any official meeting. I heard his name, but his name was not mentioned anywhere officially. I simply heard other people say there is a Colonel Beara. He is in dealing with security affairs. However, I never attended a meeting where he was present, where he spoke, where somebody introduced him. That was the first time I ever saw him. Had he not introduced himself, I wouldn't have known his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe I cleared up the matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's stick on that last point just briefly if we could. So the regular process would be to go through the Bratunac Brigade in this situation to get some heavy machines?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Corrections. Misstates the evidence. One of the ways. He cited three ways. Look at the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. One of ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One of the ways and I have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's flat out wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, please look at the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand one of the ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm saying the regular way. This is what he said. The regular way is to go through the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just use the words. One of the ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's not what he said, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can point to the record, Your Honour. Let's be fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't wish to debate the issue. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But the point is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A regular way would be to go through the Bratunac Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think that would be one of the ways, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you answered that question earlier, you weren't sure about your answer?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned three ways in my opinion. One could go through the Bratunac Brigade, too, which in my opinion would be normal, because Bratunac Brigade is in Bratunac, the Executive Board is in Bratunac, and there is communication between these two. We were not very far away from the command, so we could see each other. We had telephone communication. We could speak on the telephone. And up until then, we did not have any unclear incidents when this came to communication, communication between the municipality and the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the command could have been involved in this particular process --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Calls for speculation. Calls for speculation I don't even want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Calls for speculation, Your Honour. "Could have been." He's asking the gentlemen to speculate. He knows or he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think so. The witness answered that which in his opinion could be normal to go to the Bratunac Brigade. So if the procedure goes like that, the natural question is that whether it has to go through the commander of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not if the higher echelon --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I objection to this argument in front of the witness. This is absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If he can identify -- if these were officers from the Bratunac Brigade, I would agree but he's indicated they're not. There are no other colonels --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then I would ask that he ask to be quiet or the witness be stepped out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think you have to hold your temper a little bit. At this moment, you are talking about one of the regular ways. Since the witness has answered that question, the natural question will be followed by Mr. McCloskey. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could the -- the process have gone through the brigade that day?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this case, they did not go through the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't know where these men were before they saw you, do you?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: These two officers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I saw them for the first time there. I could have met them in the street and not know who they were. I met them for the first time in that SDS office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Listen to my question. You don't know where they were before they met you, did you?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't know who they were talking to before they met you, do you?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you don't know what they might have been talking to people about before they saw you?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: With whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't know who they might have been talking to, do you, or what they were talking about?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know these people either, let alone who they'd talk to prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you brought up the brick factory; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that the factory known as Ciglana?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the factory that manufactures brick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ciglana?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Ciglana. The company manufacturing bricks and tiles for construction of houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Deronjic speak to you about the army's plan to murder Muslim prisoners at this Ciglana factory?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, nor was it done in that factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Deronjic was chasing after Mr. Beara that very morning, 14 July, to prevent him from murdering people at the Ciglana factory?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. And as far as I know, no people were killed at Ciglana. Had it been done there, I would have heard that from someone, but as far as I know, and I can assure you of that, that wasn't done there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that the evening before this morning of the 14th, at the warehouse in Kravica, that there was a piece of heavy equipment that was working at the warehouse picking up bodies that had been murdered there?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about how that machine would have been requisitioned for use?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't even know whether the machine was requisitioned, let alone whether the machine did any work. I called the director. I told him that people would come, and he didn't tell me later whether the people had indeed come and had taken the machines. So I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But for that day, too, the 13th, the normal way of getting a machine would be involving the Bratunac Brigade, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're aiming at with your question. I've simply told you what was done regarding that. Now, as to the procedure and whether the procedure was followed, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Try to answer my question if you can. On the 13th, the day before this, there had been a normal option for anyone wanting to use a public machine to go through the Bratunac Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection to "anyone." Anyone. Who is anyone? Does that mean that Mladic, General Mladic has to go through the Bratunac Brigade or General Krstic or Borovcanin or Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. If he wants to argue his case he can do it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He needs to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's not a darn thing wrong with that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Pure obstruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The witness said they don't know the name of those two persons. He never saw those two persons in his office on that day, so I think that's why Mr. McCloskey used the word "anyone."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As long as I understand the witness's testimony that no matter who it is, Karadzic or whatever, they would have to go through the Bratunac Brigade and ask Colonel Blagojevic, if that's his testimony, then I'll sit down, but that's not how I understood it to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that the witness could give us the answer on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but he said that a person would have to go through the Bratunac Brigade. That was, of course, never part of my question, and so it may be confusing for the witness at this point. I think I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I can go on, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't say would have to but could have, if I understood you properly. I did not say would have to. The person could have gone through the Bratunac Brigade, but in this case they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that's what you testified to. Thank you. Colonel Blagojevic was born in Bratunac as well as yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you know --

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In a village by Bratunac, five or six -- five to six kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know him or his family while growing up?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know Colonel Blagojevic until his arrival in the brigade. He's younger than I am. Did he not live in town itself. He lived in a village six to seven kilometres away. We were not same generation, so I did not know him up until he was appointed commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And after that period when he was appointed commander, you did know him and have dealings with him?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said that someone asked you, I believe it was after the fall of Srebrenica, to go over to the Bratunac Brigade on the morning of the day after the fall; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you mean the first contact with General Mladic, the first time we met at the command, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I asked you whether or not someone had asked you to go to the command, not the Hotel Fontana. Did someone ask you to go to the command on the morning of the 12th of July, the day after Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the evening, Deronjic told me that I should be at the command the following morning. He said this to me on the 11th, saying that I should be there at around 8.00. It was peculiar to me that in the morning at the general's, I did not see Deronjic when it was him who had told me that I should be there the following morning. He himself did not come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you believed Deronjic must have been in touch with someone about this meeting, obviously, otherwise he couldn't have told you about it.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since he told me this, somebody must have told him to tell me this. The two of us are neighbours. I don't know who told him to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were told to go to the meeting at the Hotel Fontana at 10.00 that same day, the 12th or the day after Srebrenica fell; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you say you trusted Mladic to be telling the truth to the Muslims at that meeting, and you in fact passed that on to one of Muslims, to trust Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the impression I had, especially since the commander of the Dutch Battalion was there, his deputy, the three of us representing the civilian government. So this was an official meeting, in my mind, and I believed that things would be all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Today would you trust Mladic's word?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what Mladic's opinion is today. I have no information regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Today would you trust the word of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would not, because things were not done as was agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see him on the television on the 11th when he came in to Potocari and looked into the camera and said, "It's now time to take revenge upon the Turks in this area"?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see that, but people told me that it was on television. I personally did not watch television. I was told that he was on television. And I don't remember him saying that, but I heard that he was on television, that the camera shot him. I didn't see that on television myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: During the meeting at the Hotel Fontana, what did Mladic say, roughly, to the Muslims that were there? As best as you can recall.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: He asked them what they wanted, whether they wanted to stay in the Srebrenica area. They were very firm about not wanting to stay there, about wanting to leave. He asked them this question several times. He also said that if they wished to stay, he would guarantee freedom and safety for them in that area. They did not accept that. They were very firm in their desire to leave the area. When he asked them where they wanted to go, they said that they wanted to go towards Tuzla and Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him threaten the Muslims at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. He did not threaten them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're sure about that?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the Muslims look scared to you at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is certain that they were not comfortable there. They did not feel at ease. Now, as to whether they were afraid, I wouldn't know that. I'm sure that they were not at ease. Had I been in their shoes, I would not have felt comfortable there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't know if they were scared or not?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. They probably were, as I've said. I would have been scared. I would not have felt indifferent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You just described how frightened you were in your meeting with Mladic the previous day.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where? I was not scared. I felt uncomfortable, but I don't know what you mean when you say fear and when you say feeling uncomfortable. I was not afraid. I was perhaps uncomfortable. I was uncomfortable about his treatment of me, because at the time, I represented civilian authorities. I was President of the Executive Board. I believed that I deserved better treatment, but I was not scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when Mladic made all these -- these offers to allow people to stay or go, would you trust -- would you trust that statement today, knowing what you know, as being genuine?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it came that things happened the way they happened. I don't know whether Mladic was responsible for that, but it is likely that after everything that had happened, I wouldn't trust anyone myself. I wouldn't trust anyone except myself to ensure that things would be done as was agreed. Now, who is responsible for this, whether Mladic did it, I don't know, but nowadays I would trust only myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear Mladic condition his promises to the Muslims on whether or not their soldiers surrendered and turned in their weapons?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember a Serb representative saying at the meeting that their Muslim men in Potocari would be screened to determine if any of them were war criminals, ages 16 to 60?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that. All I know is that it was said that there was a large number of people in Potocari who were in need of assistance and that that problem needed to be resolved. So from that moment on, this was what guided me at the meeting, and I don't remember the other details, whether there were any conditions, whether somebody was to inspect it or not. I knew that it was not up to me to screen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the next two days, that large population was transported out of Potocari; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've described some of the assistance you gave those people. Did you provide that assistance on both days that this transportation took place?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Are you -- are you hearing me? Can you hear me? I was in Potocari only the first day. I wasn't there the second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't go at all on the second day?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. The second day I only passed by on my way to Srebrenica. That's where I was going, Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went there to satisfy my sheer curiosity, to see what it was like because I didn't -- I hadn't seen it since 1992, and I heard a lot about how difficult life was there. I just passed by and went on my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you go with anybody else?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The driver, the municipal service driver. We went in the service car belonging to the municipal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just you and the driver?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's the driver's name?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brano Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And his father's name, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, during the time you've described taking part in the transportation or actually helping the Muslim people on that first day, did you see any Muslim men being separated out of the crowd of people?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that Muslim men were being detained in buildings around the area where the crowd was on that day?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any abuse of the Muslim population that day?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see their belongings cast aside and piled up nearby where they were on buses?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see what belongings they had. They had perhaps some clothes, some belongings tied up in a piece of cloth. I couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see many of those belongings being cast aside and piled up in the dirt along the side of the road?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That night, were you aware that Muslim men were detained in the hangar behind the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. I knew that there was a number of people in the school building. I didn't know about the hangar. To the best of my knowledge, that hangar did not even have a roof. It was a completely demolished building, a ruin since 1992. There were no people in the hangar. There were some people in the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many people were in the school building?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think their number never went over 50. When enough people would gather to fill one bus, they would be taken out of there and put on a transport. I don't think the number ever exceeded 50. I didn't go there to look. I didn't go into the school building. I just asked the policemen who were standing outside once. That was on one occasion when I went there to see what's going on, but I didn't go inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that school building, the Vuk Karadzic school building, the same building that you referred to that became partly destroyed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I did not describe it very well. The school building as such was not destroyed in the sense that a wall had caved in or it didn't have a room -- a roof. It's just that the windows were broken and otherwise it wasn't destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But it hadn't been used since -- since 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It hadn't been used because there were two school buildings in Bratunac, and one primary school was enough to receive all the pupils we had in Bratunac. I don't think that other building would have been used even if it had been in good condition, because we didn't have enough schoolchildren to fill two schools. I think only one building was enough, because it had 24 classrooms. It was a bigger, better building than the Vuk Karadzic school. That's where the pupils went to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge, any reason to believe Muslims from Srebrenica would be very frightened about being put in the Vuk Karadzic school in July of 1995 because of what happened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims from Srebrenica were never placed in that school building. They were in Potocari. And they were not taken to Bratunac from Potocari and placed in that school. In Potocari, they were put directly on the convoys, on the transports, and the transports went through Bratunac but did not stop there, and the people from Potocari were not taken to the Vuk Karadzic school. The people who were brought to the Vuk Karadzic school were those who were captured on the road from Kravica to Konjevic Polje, who surrendered on that road, and I think that school was a collection point for such men, but even they were transported later on towards Kladanj and Tuzla, and they were treated the same way as the people in Potocari. They were transported to Tuzla just as the people from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question is, is the Muslims that stayed in the school in Bratunac in July of 1995, would they have had reason to be afraid of being in that school because of what happened in 1992 at that school?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whether they were afraid or not, I don't know, but if I had been in their shoes, I would probably be frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were Muslims placed in that school in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was not in the same position as I was in 1995. I was a regular soldier in the brigade, and I was not based in town, but I had heard that Muslims had been placed in the Vuk Karadzic school. And when I would come home on leave, I would not go close to the school. My house was elsewhere, and I was not curious enough to go and check, but I had heard that they had been placed there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you hear what had happened to them at that school in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was that? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that some of them lost their lives there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The rest were shipped out somewhere else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know that on one transport in 1992, people were taken from that school towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if you can recall, when were the most Muslims actually transported to Bratunac and spent the night? Was it that first night, which would have been 12 July, that first day that you were helping out at Potocari, or would it have been the next night, the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the buses that had come not from Potocari but from Milici to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From the direction of Milici were a number of buses, yes. That would include buses from along the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the road from Milici to Konjevic Polje to Bratunac. I think that happened in the night between the 12th and the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall the 13th, the second day of the evacuation? Is that the day when most of the people arrived, the day of the 13th in the evening, or you just don't recall?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Arrived where?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I've answered this already. The largest number arrived in the night between the 12th and the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you receive any reports of any of those Muslims being brutalised?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. Nobody made such reports available to me, and I wasn't aware of it. I didn't have these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear any reports about bodies being in Bratunac on the 14th of July around the town area and around the schools and around where the vehicles had been parked?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that some corpses were left behind in the school building. I cannot give you a number, but it's true that some remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who did you hear this from?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly from whom I heard this, but I did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When? When did you hear about it? When did you hear about corpses at this Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you the date or the time of day, but it was probably when it was all over, when everybody had left, when the school building was empty, and that was probably after the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you follow up on it? Did you report it to the police?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the police were certainly better informed than I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you do anything to report these corpses?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't report to anyone, nor was it my job. To whom was I supposed to report to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know any effort to let UNPROFOR in to the schools or around the vehicles in Bratunac to help take care of the Muslims, some of whom were corpses, by the morning of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't recall. Maybe it's because I'm tired, but I don't recall there's been evidence with respect to UNPROFOR trying to get there. I might be mistaken, but I don't recall that there's been testimony in the Prosecution's case in chief with respect to that last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Lay some foundations for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can -- I know it's been a long trial, but one testified that he followed buses to the area in front of the Vuk Karadzic school and -- full of Muslim men and was arrested and removed from his vehicle and had his material taken away from him and sent -- sent packing, basically. However, the question really doesn't need a foundation. I'm just asking him if there was any effort made by anyone to let UNPROFOR protect the people that they had the mandate to protect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you or anyone else that you knew make any effort to contact UNPROFOR and get them to help these people at the schools and parked around the town?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I saw those buses, those vehicles only the evening. I did what I could to help. I gave them some water. And in the morning they were already gone. Nobody required me to submit any reports, and it wasn't my obligation to do so. I had no communication whatsoever with any higher level authority such as the Assembly of Republika Srpska. I did not have that chain of coordination, and I don't see to whom I could have reported and what.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you or anyone else you were aware of try to call the Red Cross or the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees to try and go help these Muslims in Bratunac in what you described as stifling heat?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that President Simic did something about that. He normally contacted the UNHCR because he had personal acquaintances among them, and he also knew that Russian man who at the time headed the UNHCR office, and he was in touch with them. I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned to Mr. Ruez a long time ago that some Muslims were coming in to Bratunac, and they were -- they were detained by the police and then moved into the various schools. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That they arrived in Bratunac and the police detained them in various schools? I didn't say that. I didn't say various schools. What I said is that there had been cases when a smaller number of Muslims found themselves in Bratunac. How or why, I don't know, but there were four or five such cases. And such men would be taken to the school building, but they would be then transferred on by buses. But that it was a common occurrence for Muslim men to be detained in school buildings, in various school buildings, I didn't say anything of the sort. I said there were some of them detained in the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I didn't mean to imply that was a common occurrence, but there were Muslims that were detained coming into Bratunac and -- by the police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you now talking about July 1995 only?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct. That's true that there were a couple of cases when the police, upon finding a Muslim man in town, would take the man into custody and detain him in the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall Mr. Ruez asking you if you knew anything about an incident at Kravica when he interviewed you a long time ago?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am not getting any translation. Can you hear me? Yes, yes, I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We can try it again. Sometimes there's little glitches. Do you recall Mr. Ruez asking you whether or not you had any information about an incident that happened in Kravica in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I get some translation now? I'm not getting any translation -- interpretation, rather.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you hear me okay now?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear well now. Yes. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. I think we're back on line. Do you remember Mr. Ruez asking you whether or not you had any information about an incident in Kravica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have a statement that I gave. I can't claim with certainty that I can remember everything I stated then because it's been a while ago, but you can see yourself what the statement says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me give you a chance to look at a small part of at that statement, if we could. It's in the B/C/S, page 15. It should be lines 2 and 3. If you could take a look. And in the English it should be page 13 and 14, lines 34, 35, and then number 1 on page 14. Just find that spot if you can. You can see it's been highlighted. Take a look at the page before and after if you want to try to orient yourself.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you can see there that Mr. Ruez says: "Did you receive any information from local officials in Kravica about the events which might have occurred in that place?" And you say: "No." And you never mention anything about any knowledge of the Kravica murders. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true that he asked me whether I received anything from the local officials in Kravica. However, there were no local officials in Kravica. Kravica did not have a mayor at the time. Kravica was a deserted settlement at the time. It was not populated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But you never --

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: And there were no local officials there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I understand that you were telling Mr. Ruez that you received no information from local officials. And did you choose not to tell him about what you knew about the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, but he asked me about local officials, and I said that I did not receive anything from them because there were no local officials there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you didn't tell him anything about what you heard about the murders at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've told us today that you know about the reburial of bodies from Glogova; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've testified that you knew some of the villages where they were taken, the victims, that is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell me the names of the villages you know that served as graves for the victims from Glogova?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I just know about Glogova. I don't know how to explain this to you. Glogova is a large area, and I don't know the villages in the vicinity of Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know where the victims from the Glogova mass grave were taken to?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the location, but I heard that they were moved to the Srebrenica area. I don't know the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever report this location to anyone so that those bodies could be found?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. That wasn't done in July of 1995. That was done, as far as I can remember, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever report, from July 1995 until the present, to anyone, including international agencies, that you knew that bodies had been taken from Glogova to somewhere by Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not convey this to anyone because I hadn't seen this. I only heard about this. Nobody informed me that this would be done. This was more in the line of speculation. Nobody told me that this was going on or that this would be done or where it would be done. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were asked earlier about your statement with respect to Kravica, and the question was, as was read to you: "Did you receive any information from local officials in Kravica about events which might have occurred in that place?" Now -- and then you stated: "No." But then you go on to say there's no mayor in Kravica; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So when Mr. Ruez was asking you the question, asking you from local officials in Kravica, was it your understanding that he was asking you if local authorities from the Kravica village had given you any information? Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then later on you do talk about Kravica, how it was burned down and how 155 people in Kravica, on Christmas Day, had been killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have to further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Gospodin Davidovic, have you had any contacts with Colonel Blagojevic in your official capacity or privately during the critical days in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I did not see Colonel Blagojevic, and I had no contacts with him, either official or private ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: One more question. Have you any information indicating that Colonel Blagojevic was involved in the murder operation that occurred in the Srebrenica enclave in July 1995 and resulted in the death of thousands of Muslim able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have no information to that effect on any participation of Colonel Blagojevic in those events. I have never heard from anyone about any kind of his involvement in crimes from 1995 until today. I never heard that he actively participated in that with others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Hvala. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: SRBISLAV DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There are no more questions out of the Judges' questions. At this stage are there any documents to tender? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, thank you, Witness, for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room when this session is closed. The hearing of today is adjourned, and we will see you Monday afternoon in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of April, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
